title: ME06c: Strength Training = Practices
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Claydon continues his Maya Essays series by recasting leadership development as strength training, the first dimension of what he calls the Leadership Gym in his Leadership, Rewritten framework. He argues that capacity for complexity is built through repeated daily practices, not seminars or inspiring mantras. He maps the four quadrants of the Praxis Q model onto muscle groups: Adaptive Growth as the core, Relational Influence as chest and shoulders, Strategic Fluency as the back, and Disciplined Delivery as the legs. The fictional leader Maya first relied on charisma and found that each unstrained muscle buckled under strategy shifts, crises and deadlines until she began deliberate reps. The piece closes with reflection prompts, a mini-diagnostic and a preview of endurance, flexibility and whole-body dimensions still to come.
points: Leadership development sells inspiration, which is a single lift, when what builds capacity is boring, consistent repetition.
The four quadrants work as muscle groups, so neglecting one leaves a leader lopsided and overtraining one risks injury.
Maya's reliance on charisma masked weak core, back and legs, which showed up only when strategy shifted, crises hit and deadlines mounted.
Each muscle has a concrete small rep, such as five minutes of reflection after a meeting or delivering one small promise on time.
Strength is only the first of four dimensions, with endurance, flexibility and integration still needed to avoid burnout, snapping or pulling apart.
quotes: You don’t become strong enough for complexity by attending a two-day seminar or by repeating a single inspiring mantra. You become strong by practicing — over and over, until the moves of leadership become as natural as lifting your own arm.
Every athlete knows: without a strong core, everything else wobbles. Adaptive Growth is leadership’s stabiliser. It’s what allows you to bend without breaking, to hold your centre when systems shift.
Relational Influence is leadership’s upper body — your visible strength. The reps here are in listening, negotiating, boundary-setting, building trust.
When strategy shifted, her core buckled. When crises hit, her back wasn’t strong enough to carry the load. When deadlines mounted, her legs weren’t trained to keep the team moving.

The problem with most leadership development is that it sells inspiration. But inspiration is a single lift — impressive, but fleeting. Strength is built in the boring, consistent reps leaders almost never celebrate.
Strength in leadership doesn’t come from charisma or insight. It comes from balanced training across your whole leadership body — core, chest, back, and legs — until the moves become muscle memory.
